editorialPurpose: Understand two people’s strategy, the constraints it created, and the danger that survived arrival in the North.
storyAngle: Their identity inversion opened travel but created new tests; illness was functional and passage remained precarious.

segments.text: In 1848, Ellen and William Craft escaped slavery by traveling openly.
Ellen posed as a white male slaveholder. Her husband, William, posed as her enslaved servant.
But that identity created a dangerous problem. A gentleman might be asked to sign his name. Ellen could not write.
So she bound her right hand, making it appear injured. A report published weeks after their escape describes her avoiding signatures this way.
Their later book explains more: bandages hid her beardless chin, spectacles obscured her face, and apparent illness gave her a reason to avoid conversation.
William helped sustain the performance, acting as her attendant. Together, they traveled north by train and steamer.
But before Philadelphia, they faced a test the disguise could not answer.
In their account, officials in Baltimore demanded assurance that the supposed master had the right to take William along.
Looking like a slaveholder was not proof of ownership.
William’s account says a conductor confirmed they had arrived on his train. With departure approaching, the officer allowed them through, citing the apparent master’s illness.
They reached Philadelphia after four days. Yet escape did not mean lasting safety.
In 1850, men came to Boston to recapture them. The Crafts subsequently left for England.
Their plan exploited the treatment given to a supposed white gentleman. But every accommodation depended on keeping that false identity intact.
They escaped a system that treated them as property, by making it appear that one owned the other.
